Title: #NSTviral: Motorcyclists running red light spark public anger on social media
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: A video showing a group of motorcyclists allegedly running a red light has drawn criticism from social media users, who condemned the act as irresponsible and dangerous.
In the 16-second clip uploaded on the DashCam Malaysia Facebook group, the group of motorcyclists can be seen ignoring the safety of other road users travelling from the opposite direction.
It is believed that the incident took place in Terengganu, although the exact location, date and time of the incident could not be verified as of press time.
Several users criticised the motorcyclists' actions, saying such behaviour could put other road users at risk and burden emergency responders if an accident occurred.
"Who would be at fault (if an untoward accident happened)? If anything happened, you would only trouble people in KKM (Health Ministry)," a user commented.
Another user questioned whether enforcement action would be taken against such road offences.
"Lawless state? Who can uphold the law?" user Lim Sg commented.
Meanwhile, another user, Mo Iedil, described the actions as a reflection of poor road discipline and mentality.
The video surfaced amid heightened public attention over road safety following several accidents, including fatal crashes, involving some motorcyclists travelling to and from the RXZ Members 8.0 gathering.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: DAP's Steven Sim dismisses Pas confidence of winning Penang
Article:
GEORGE TOWN: Penang DAP chief Steven Sim has dismissed Pas' confidence of winning Penang in the next election, describing the remarks as "arrogant".
Responding to remarks by Pas information chief
Ahmad Fadhli Shaari
that the current political wave would also see the party capture Penang in the next general election, Sim said such statements reflected overconfidence.
"I saw reports in the media that Perikatan Nasional leaders from Pas are saying they are riding a political wave. Not only do they believe they will continue winning in the states they already control, they are also claiming they will win Penang. Have you read that? You have, right?
"Some people asked me, as DAP Penang chief, what my response is. My answer is simple. They are winning now. Yes, let them be confident because they are winning at the moment. They have become arrogant and conceited, and so they are making arrogant statements," he said during the Tanjung@40 dinner here late last night.
Sim said, as far as he was concerned, the answer was straightforward.
"Let them remain with their arrogance. Penang DAP and Penang Pakatan Harapan will continue working hard to safeguard and defend the state of Penang, as well as every DAP and Pakatan Harapan seat.
"That is my response to them," he added.
Fadhli, in a personal commentary on his social media page, alleged that the Pakatan Harapan government was already on its last legs.
He said it was only a matter of time before it fell.
"Once Parliament is dissolved, the PH bloc can prepare to take over the opposition benches.
"If the BN (Barisan Nasional)-PN formula can be carried into the next general election, every state in Peninsular Malaysia, including Penang, can be won. Therefore, PN and BN leaders should not look back. Continue with this winning formula. Do not be distracted by Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim's Hari Raya reconciliation calls. Continue serving professionally under the current government until Parliament is dissolved.
"Friends in PH should reflect on why the people are rejecting you today. Do not blame us by suggesting that voters have been misled by racial sentiments. Do you really think the people are not intelligent?" he said.
Yesterday, Juasseh assemblyman
Datuk Ismail Lasim
was sworn in as the 12th Menteri Besar of Negri Sembilan.
BN won 18 of the 36 state seats, while PN secured seven, allowing the two coalitions to form the new state government with a combined 25-seat majority.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Airline strike in Canada grounds estimated 250,000 passengers
Article:
TRENTON: More than 4,000 flight attendants at WestJet, Canada's second-largest airline, went on strike Sunday, grounding about 600 daily flights and disrupting travel plans for an estimated 250,000 passengers, Anadolu Ajansi reported.
Monday is a civic holiday in Canada, making it one of the busiest travel weekends of the year. The strike is expected to cost WestJet millions of dollars.
Pay is at the centre of the dispute. Flight attendants are seeking compensation for work performed on the ground before and after flights.
Delta Air Lines became the first airline to introduce pay for ground work in 2022. Air Canada followed in February under a new contract.
Federal Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu said in a social media post that she was disappointed the two sides had failed to reach an agreement after trying to negotiate a new contract.
The flight attendants are members of the Canadian Union of Public Employees. In a statement, union representative Alia Hussain blamed WestJet for the strike.
"We would not be here if (the airline) had taken our concerns seriously for almost 11 months of bargaining," Hussain said.
WestJet said affected passengers would receive refunds.
"We're disappointed to be here; this directly impacts the travel plans of our guests, our WestJetters and the communities and businesses we serve," CEO Alexis von Hoensbroech told The Canadian Press.
Flight attendants currently earn between $28.88 and $53.61 per credit hour.
Under Air Canada's new agreement, flight attendants receive compensation of up to 70 per cent of their hourly rate for the hour before takeoff.

Title: UK faces recession if Strait of Hormuz stays closed
Article:
LONDON: Britain's economy is likely to shrink in 2027 if the Strait of Hormuz does not reopen to shipping before the middle of next year, forecasters at accountants EY warned on Monday.
EY slightly nudged up its growth forecast for this year to 0.8 per cent from 0.9 per cent, on the basis that the Strait reopens by the end of September, and sees growth of 1.2 per cent in 2027 on that basis.
"If the Strait of Hormuz reopens in the coming months, we expect the UK to avoid a more pronounced downturn, but an extended closure into 2027 would raise inflation and could push the economy into contraction next year," EY UK Chief Economist Peter Arnold said.
* EY predicts that if the Strait of Hormuz remains shut until early to mid 2027, UK growth this year will slow to 0.5 per cent and that the economy will shrink 0.2 per cent in 2027
* Inflation is likely to rise to 6.4 per cent by the end of 2026 under that scenario, compared with a lower peak of 3. per cent this year if the Strait reopens in the next couple of months
* Bank of England forecasts last week, under an adverse scenario where oil and gas prices remain 30 per cent-60 per cent higher than markets expect, still showed the economy growing by close to 1.0 per cent next year while quarterly inflation peaked at 4.5 per cent
* EY expects the BoE to keep interest rates on hold this year and then cut them next year from 3.75 per cent to 3.25 per cent with moves in April and July
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Gold gains as oil slumps after Trump holds off on Iran attack
Article:
BENGALURU: Gold rose on Monday as oil prices tumbled after US President Donald Trump held off on a fresh attack on Iran in hopes of a swift deal, slightly easing concerns about inflation and higher interest rates.
FUNDAMENTALS
* Spot gold was up 0.7 per cent at US$4,067.06 per ounce, as of 0023 GMT. US gold futures rose 0.9 per cent to US$4,065.60.
* Trump said late on Saturday on his Truth Social platform that Iran and other Middle Eastern countries had asked for time to complete a deal that would lead to "the Immediate, Complete and Total" reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and "an end to Iran's nuclear threat".
* Oil prices fell more than US$5 a barrel at Monday's open.
* Gold has come under pressure since the start of the US-Iran conflict, as a war-driven rise in inflation could prompt central banks to raise interest rates. Although bullion is traditionally viewed as a hedge against inflation, its appeal tends to diminish in a high-interest-rate environment because it does not yield interest.
* Three Federal Reserve officials who dissented at last week's policy meeting in favour of an interest rate hike expressed concern on Friday that without an immediate increase in short-term borrowing costs, inflation will stay stuck above the Fed's 2 per cent target, where it has been for more than five years.
* Market participants will also focus on a slew of US jobs reports due this week, including job openings data, the ADP employment report, weekly jobless claims and the nonfarm payrolls report.
* Spot silver gained 0.7 per cent to US$58.02 per ounce, platinum climbed 0.7 per cent to US$1,653.78, and palladium firmed 1.5 per cent to US$1,293.00.
* Russia's Norilsk Nickel, the world's largest palladium producer, reported on Friday that its revenue and net profit in the first six months had sharply increased.

Title: Chery to invest US$75mil in Korea's KG Mobility, eyes overseas markets
Article:
SEOUL: China's Chery Automobile has agreed to invest US$75 million in South Korean automaker KG Mobility Corp through convertible bonds, KG Mobility said. If converted into shares, the bonds would give Chery a stake of about 10 per cent in the company.
"Chery has many manufacturing bases around the world. We believe these locations could become key areas for future cooperation between our two companies. For example, we could explore sharing global production capacity and collaborating across various aspects of manufacturing," Zhang Guibing, president of Chery International, told reporters in Seoul.
"We also see many other opportunities for cooperation, including distribution channels and even brand-related collaboration," he said.
Chinese automakers are increasingly partnering with established carmakers to make use of underutilised overseas factories.
"One of our key objectives is, of course, to strengthen our presence in overseas markets," said Zhang. Chery is China's largest car exporter.
Chery is actively exploring various options for entering the US market, Zhang said, adding that it would need to comply with a wide range of US laws, regulations and other requirements before doing so.
KG Mobility is on track to launch a midsize SUV, codenamed SE-10, in January using Chery's T2X vehicle platform. Petrol and plug-in hybrid versions will be available for domestic and overseas markets.
The company has no current plans to export the model to the US market, but remains open to the possibility, KG Mobility Chairman Kwak Jae-sun said.
KG Mobility, formerly known as SsangYong Motor, ranks behind Hyundai, Kia and General Motors in South Korea. The SUV maker sold more than 55,000 vehicles in South Korea and overseas in the first half of the year, with exports accounting for about 60 per cent of total sales.
The two companies also agreed to form a task force to explore cooperation in semiconductors, robotics, raw materials, steel and other areas, Kwak said.

Title: Ringgit opens higher against US dollar ahead of key US economic data
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: The ringgit opened slightly higher against the US dollar on Monday ahead of the release of key United States (US) economic data today amid easing tensions in Middle East.
At 8am, the local currency edged up to 4.0805/0900 against the greenback from last Friday's close of  4.0835/0875.
Bank Muamalat Malaysia Bhd chief economist Dr Mohd Afzanizam Abdul Rashid said the US Institute for Supply Management (ISM) Manufacturing PMI for July will be released tonight, with the consensus estimate at 54.0, which is higher than June's reading of 53.3.
"Additionally, uncertainties over the Middle East conflict also weighed on market sentiment, with Brent crude oil rising 4.59 per cent to US$88.10 per barrel.
"President Donald Trump reportedly said over the weekend that he has cancelled the planned military strikes against Iran as both countries are expected to reach a deal on the nuclear programme and the full reopening of the Strait of Hormuz," he told Bernama.
However, Mohd Afzanizam said the market remains cautious; thus, the local note is expected to trade within a narrow range of RM4.07 to RM4.09 today.
Meanwhile, SPI Asset Management managing partner Stephen Innes said the US dollar weakened after Trump cancelled the planned strike on Iran over the weekend.
He said the decision has sent oil prices and inflation breakevens lower, pulling down the US interest-rate curve.
"That combination should be supportive for the ringgit and, more broadly, for risk assets across Asia today," he added.
The ringgit traded lower against a basket of major currencies at the opening.
It slipped against the Japanese yen to 2.5880/5942 from 2.5520/5548 at last Friday's close, fell versus the euro to 4.7089/7199 from 4.6981/7027 and depreciated against the British pound to 5.5038/5166 from 5.4923/4977.
Against regional currencies, the ringgit traded mixed.
It gained against the Indonesian rupiah to  226.4/227.0 from 226.6/226.8 and rose versus the Thai baht to 12.2211/2558 from 12.2264/2435.
However, it softened against the Singapore dollar to 3.1844/1921 from 3.1823/1856 and was little changed versus the Philippine peso to 6.66/6.68 from 6.66/6.67.

Title: Oil tumbles as Trump cancels attack on Iran to reach nuclear deal
Article:
SINGAPORE: Oil prices tumbled US$4 a barrel on Monday after US President Donald Trump held off on a fresh attack on Iran, seeking to reach a quick deal that would halt Tehran's nuclear ambitions and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
Brent crude futures slid US$4.08, or 4.64 per cent, to US$83.85 by 2352 GMT while US West Texas Intermediate crude was at US$80.66 a barrel, down US$4.01, or 4.74 per cent.
Both contracts jumped more than 20 per cent last month after fighting between the US and Iran resumed and as attacks on several tankers around Oman heightened security concerns, deterring shippers from entering the Gulf to load oil. In a sign of de-escalation, Trump said late on Saturday on his Truth Social platform that Iran and other Middle Eastern countries had asked for time to complete a deal that would lead to "the Immediate, Complete and Total" reopening of the vital strait and "an end to Iran's nuclear threat".
"The bigger focus is whether this week turns into a rinse and repeat of last week — with hopes of a deal collapsing as Iran digs in its heels and continues to leverage its control over the Strait, potentially through an attack on a US base or a tanker transiting the waterway," IG market analyst Tony Sycamore said.
Two tankers laden with Saudi oil crossed the Bab el-Mandeb Strait out of the Red Sea over the weekend while traffic in the Strait of Hormuz slowed following reports of vessel attacks, shipping data showed on Monday. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations has reported three more tanker attacks since Saturday.
On Sunday, OPEC+ approved an oil production quota increase of around 188,000 barrels per day from September, the producer group said, in a move that completes the unwinding of a layer of voluntary output cuts.
Due to export disruptions from the Gulf, Russia and Kazakhstan caused by the Iran and Ukraine wars, successive monthly OPEC+ hikes over most of this year have remained largely on paper with little impact on the market.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Peru probes crash of tourist plane that killed 13
Article:
LIMA: Peruvian authorities said on Sunday they are investigating the crash of a small plane carrying tourists to view the famous Nazca Lines, which killed all 13 people on board.
Seven Italians, two Germans and two Spaniards died, along with two Peruvian crew members, when their Cessna 208 Caravan aircraft crashed on Saturday after it took off from the airport in Pisco, located about 240 kilometres (150 miles) south of the capital Lima.
A grim recovery process continued overnight, with police placing charred bodies in black bags for transport to the regional morgue.
Once procedures at the crash site are completed, the investigation will be carried out "in coordination with the relevant authorities to determine the causes of this tragic plane crash", the Public Prosecutor's Office said in a statement.
Due to the condition in which the bodies were recovered, "DNA tests will be conducted, which will allow for the scientific identification of the victims so their remains can be returned to their families".
It remained unclear why the plane went down, although Foreign Trade Minister Rogers Valencia told reporters that "the pilot reported mechanical problems before the crash", adding that it had yet to be determined whether there was an engine failure.
"The plane exploded, apparently as a result of the impact; it did not explode beforehand," said Carlos Cordero of the Transportation Ministry's aviation accident investigation commission.
Early Sunday, Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni offered her "deepest condolences for the tragic plane crash in Peru, in which seven Italian citizens lost their lives".
The plane was operated by AeroDiana, which offers sightseeing trips over the Nazca Lines.
The company expressed regret over the accident and stated it was "fully cooperating with the competent authorities, making all required information available to assist in the ongoing investigations".
The Nazca Lines are best seen from the air, and deadly crashes have occurred in the past. In a 2022 crash, seven people were killed, including three Dutch nationals.
The archaeological site features geoglyphs etched into the desert sands that date back to between 500 BC and 500 AD.

Title: Four Al-Fayed survivors told they were trafficking victims
Article:
LONDON: Four women who allege abuse by late Harrods owner Mohamed Al-Fayed have been confirmed as victims of human trafficking by the UK's Interior Ministry, a group representing the survivors told AFP on Monday.
The former business tycoon, who died in 2023 without facing any prosecution, has been accused by dozens of women of assault, rape and human trafficking over a period of more than three decades.
Many worked on the shop floor at Harrods in London or were hired as assistants at his various businesses, including the Ritz hotel in Paris.
Four women, who use the pseudonyms Isabella, Justine, Elizabeth and Margo and founded the "No One Above" advocacy group, have now been recognised as victims of human trafficking.
Their experiences, dating from the 1990s to after 2010, include international and domestic trafficking, Isabella confirmed in emails to AFP.
They were referred to the National Referral Mechanism (NRM), Britain's official framework to identify and support victims of human trafficking and modern slavery, by the Unseen UK charity.
The four received "conclusive grounds" decisions that they were victims between May and July.
The BBC reported in April that a fifth woman, Rachael Louw, was confirmed as a victim of human trafficking after reporting being abused by Fayed and his brother Salah in the UK and France.
Isabella, who worked in Fayed's Harrods office in 2001, said she was recognised as a trafficking victim in May.
"This was one bad man, but he couldn't have done what he did without Harrods processing women to him and silencing them afterwards," she told the Press Association news agency, which first reported the trafficking referral decisions.
POLICE PROBES
To date, 157 victims have reported allegations that they were sexually assaulted, raped or trafficked by the former tycoon to London's Metropolitan Police.
Dozens more who worked at his luxury department store have filed for compensation under a redress scheme set up after a 2024 BBC documentary revealed the scale of his alleged offences.
The Met has so far questioned six people suspected of enabling Fayed's offences, although it has not made any arrests. Some of them were questioned on suspicion of human trafficking for sexual exploitation.
Some victims, including Louw, have expressed frustration that the Met is not focusing on the trafficking aspect of the alleged offences.
Earlier this year, Louw told AFP she had instead turned to France, where a police investigation into Mohamed and Salah Fayed's abuse is being handled by a human trafficking unit.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Why Malaysia's regional economies remain weakly integrated
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia is politically and administratively integrated, but its production economy remains considerably less integrated.
The country shares a common currency, national financial institutions, federal taxation, uniform regulations and extensive transport and communications infrastructure. Goods, capital and labour generally move freely across state boundaries. Yet administrative unity alone does not create economic interdependence.
A truly integrated economy is one in which firms across regions purchase inputs from one another, exchange technology, provide specialised services and participate in shared value chains. Growth in one state should generate investment, employment and demand elsewhere through supplier networks rather than remain confined within isolated industrial clusters.
Malaysia has achieved this only partially. Strong production ecosystems remain concentrated in the Klang Valley, the Penang-Kedah electronics corridor and the Johor-Singapore economic region. Sabah and Sarawak are major contributors to the national economy, but much of their production continues to revolve around commodities, energy and primary processing, with relatively limited downstream integration into wider Malaysian supply chains. Malaysia therefore appears economically connected while remaining structurally fragmented.
What Input-Output Analysis Reveals
Regional Input-Output (RIO) analysis offers a more accurate way to understand this fragmentation.
Input-output tables record how industries buy from and sell to one another. Their technical coefficients measure the quantity of inputs required to produce each unit of output. Extended across regions, they reveal whether firms source components, services and technology domestically or rely on imports.
Strong interregional coefficients indicate production networks that span the country. Weak coefficients suggest that states function largely as parallel economies, each linked more closely to international markets than to one another.
Malaysia's 2021 national input-output table recorded RM2.097 trillion of intermediate transactions, equivalent to 45.3 per cent of total supply, confirming the importance of inter-industry production. However, national tables do not identify where those transactions occur geographically. They cannot reveal whether industries in Penang purchase inputs from Sarawak, whether Sabah sources packaging from Selangor or whether petrochemical production in Bintulu supports manufacturers elsewhere in Malaysia.
Without regularly published regional and interregional input-output tables, policymakers cannot accurately measure domestic value chains, identify import leakages or determine where infrastructure and industrial policies would generate the greatest national multiplier. This limits the effectiveness of regional development policy.
Connected Globally, Less Connected Domestically
Malaysia is one of the world's most open trading economies, with total trade reaching approximately 136.4 per cent of GDP in 2025. Yet global integration should not be mistaken for domestic integration.
A manufacturer may import sophisticated components from East Asia, assemble products in Penang and export them to Europe or the United States. While fully integrated into global value chains, it may generate relatively limited spillovers if few inputs, services or technologies are sourced from other Malaysian regions.
As Bank Negara Malaysia has noted, domestic value added provides a better measure of how much income, technology and industrial capability remain within the national economy. Malaysia's challenge is therefore not participation in global value chains but strengthening domestic production networks beneath them.
Advanced industrial economies combine global openness with dense domestic supplier ecosystems linking manufacturers, engineering firms, logistics providers, research institutions and specialised service companies across multiple regions.
Malaysia possesses important regional strengths—Penang in electronics, Johor in manufacturing and logistics, the Klang Valley in finance and advanced services, Sarawak in energy and petrochemicals, and Sabah in agriculture, fisheries and tourism. The weakness lies not in these capabilities themselves, but in the production linkages connecting them.
Import Leakage and Weak Domestic Multipliers
Import leakage occurs when rising domestic demand is satisfied by foreign rather than Malaysian suppliers.
Imports of advanced machinery and technology are often necessary and beneficial. The problem arises when domestic industries remain unable to supply inputs that could reasonably be produced competitively within Malaysia.
Large investments may increase GDP while generating relatively modest domestic multipliers if engineering services, specialised machinery, digital systems and maintenance contracts are largely imported. Similarly, states exporting raw materials while importing processed products and industrial inputs create growth without sufficiently deep industrial capability.
The appropriate response is not protectionism but supplier development. Public procurement, industrial incentives and investment approvals should increasingly support vendor development, workforce upgrading, technology transfer and domestic sourcing wherever commercially viable.
Why Economic Corridors Have Fallen Short
Malaysia's economic corridors—including the Northern Corridor Economic Region, East Coast Economic Region, Iskandar Malaysia, Sabah Development Corridor and Sarawak Corridor of Renewable Energy—have expanded infrastructure and attracted investment. Yet infrastructure alone does not create production networks.
Highways, ports and industrial parks facilitate economic activity but do not automatically generate supplier relationships or domestic value creation. Successful regional development depends on industrial capabilities, skilled labour, strong institutions and close coordination between public investment and private production.
Corridors should therefore be evaluated not only by investment commitments, infrastructure or employment, but also by procurement from Malaysian firms, cross-state supplier participation, technology transfer and domestic value added. These indicators measure production integration rather than administrative implementation.
Regional Divergence Is a Structural Warning
A recent World Bank assessment found that regional income disparities remain pronounced, with richer states generally growing faster than poorer ones. This reflects differences in productivity, industrial concentration, skills and production connectivity rather than simply variations in fiscal transfers.
Regions with stronger production ecosystems continue attracting firms because suppliers, workers and supporting industries are already present. Regions without those networks struggle to generate similar momentum. Fiscal transfers remain important for equity and infrastructure, but on their own they cannot create the production linkages needed for sustained regional convergence.
From State Projects to National Value Chains
Malaysia's next stage of regional policy should therefore treat the country as a single production system rather than a collection of competing investment destinations.
First, regional and interregional input-output tables should be compiled and published regularly to measure interstate trade, domestic sourcing, value-added retention and import leakages.
Second, major investment projects receiving public incentives should include national supply-chain development plans that create procurement opportunities for firms across Malaysia.
Third, regional specialisation should become complementary rather than duplicative. Sarawak's energy resources, Penang's electronics ecosystem, Johor's logistics platform, Sabah's bio-resources and the Klang Valley's financial and professional services should operate as integrated components of national value chains.
Finally, logistics policy, universities, technical institutions and research centres should be aligned with industrial supply chains so that skills development supports actual production requirements.
Building Economic Interdependence
Malaysia does not lack regional strengths. It lacks sufficient mechanisms to connect them.
Administrative federalism created a functioning nation-state. Fiscal federalism established systems for raising and distributing public revenue. The next stage is production federalism—an economy in which the prosperity of one region increasingly depends upon, and contributes to, the productive capacity of another.
The objective is not economic self-sufficiency but stronger domestic integration within an open economy. A nation becomes truly integrated when its firms, technologies, suppliers and workers are connected through production.
Malaysia has largely achieved administrative integration. Its next national task is to build genuine production integration—connecting firms, suppliers, technologies and workers across regions so that growth in one part of the country increasingly generates prosperity throughout the whole economy.

Title: The end of the command-and-control CEO
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: The greatest test of a chief executive officer (CEO) is not whether an organisation succeeds because of them, but whether it can continue succeeding without them. Around the world, organisations are quietly rewriting the rules of management. Layers of hierarchy are disappearing; decisions are moving closer to customers and employees are increasingly trusted to exercise their judgement. As authority shifts away from the boardroom, an important question emerges: what is the changing role of the Chief Executive Officer?
For decades, a CEO's success was measured by familiar metrics—strategy, revenue growth, profitability, capital allocation and risk management. Those responsibilities remain vital. Yet in an era of flatter organisations, they are no longer enough. Increasingly, a CEO's success will be judged not only by the strategy they craft but also by the organisation they create to bring that strategy to life.
At first glance, flatter organisations appear to reduce the importance of the CEO. After all, if employees are making more decisions, what remains for the person at the top? In reality, the CEO's role becomes even more important—but fundamentally different. Rather than making every critical decision, the CEO designs an organisation that enables thousands of good decisions to be made every day.
Empowering employees does not mean abandoning leadership. It means redesigning leadership. Instead of becoming the organisation's chief decision-maker, the CEO becomes its chief designer-shaping the structure, culture and decision-making systems that enable people closest to customers to respond with speed, confidence and accountability.
Like an architect who designs a building rather than laying every brick, the CEO designs the organisation rather than making every operational decision. An architect determines how different parts of a building connect and ensures that the finished structure is functional, resilient and capable of serving its intended purpose. Likewise, a CEO creates an organisation in which people, processes and systems work together effectively to achieve organisational goals.
The CEO must also ensure that communication flows freely throughout the organisation and that reliable, timely information reaches those responsible for making decisions. This enables employees to respond quickly while remaining accountable for their actions. The most enduring legacy of a CEO is therefore not merely the strategy they formulate, but the organisation they build. Their success is ultimately measured by whether the organisation can continue making sound decisions and executing strategy without constant intervention from the top.
A brilliant strategy is no guarantee of success. Many organisations possess sound strategies yet struggle because decision-making is slow, bureaucracy dominates and departments operate in silos. Where employees fear making mistakes or are discouraged from taking initiative, innovation declines and execution suffers. The challenge is therefore not the strategy itself but whether the organisation has been designed to execute it effectively.
This is where organisation design becomes one of a CEO's most important responsibilities. Great organisations do not emerge by accident; they are deliberately designed. The CEO decides how authority is distributed, how information flows, who makes decisions, how leaders behave, how people are rewarded and how talent is developed. Together, these elements shape not only how work gets done, but also how quickly an organisation can adapt, solve problems, innovate and execute its strategy.
Few leaders demonstrate the power of organisational design better than Satya Nadella. When he became the CEO of Microsoft in 2014, he inherited a company widely regarded as bureaucratic, internally competitive and slow to respond to changing customer needs. Rather than beginning with products or technology, Nadella began by transforming the company's culture. He encouraged managers to become coaches, developers of people, facilitators and removers of obstacles. He also broke down organisational silos and encouraged collaboration across many divisions such as Azure, Office, Windows, Xbox and Research. He fostered a learning culture where employees were encouraged to ask questions, experiment and learn continuously. He adopted the principle of learn-it-all" rather than know-it-all". Microsoft's resurgence demonstrates that organisational transformation often begins with culture rather than strategy alone.
Another example that illustrates that organisational design is about structure and systems, not just leadership style, is Nucor. Under former CEO Ken Iverson, Nucor built a lean organisational structure with few management layers and delegated significant operational decision-making authority to its plants while empowering frontline employees to solve problems close to where they occurred. Rather than centralising operational decisions at headquarters, plant managers were given considerable autonomy.
Employees were encouraged to improve productivity, suggest innovations and take ownership of results through a performance-based incentive system. Managers were expected to support employees, remove operational obstacles and enable teams to perform effectively rather than closely supervise routine activities. Nucor demonstrates that organisational success is not achieved by concentrating authority at the top but by designing systems that empower people throughout the organisation.
As Malaysia seeks to attract investment and innovation-driven industries and position itself as the preferred location for Asean regional headquarters, organisational design can become one of Malaysia's competitive advantages. Malaysian CEOs must move beyond managing the day-to-day operations and become architects of organisations that are agile, empowering and capable of executing strategy. Ultimately, the organisations that will thrive are not those with the tallest hierarchies, but those that are best designed to unlock the potential of their people.

Title: Home-grown firms rewrite Malaysia's export story
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysian-owned companies are emerging as a powerful force behind the country's export growth, reshaping the narrative that high-value exports are driven largely by multinational corporations.
Malaysia External Trade Development Corp (Matrade) chairman Datuk Seri Reezal Merican Naina Merican said Malaysia's deep integration into global value chains has long created the perception that foreign multinationals are the main engines of export success.
But Matrade's latest half-year analysis reveals a broader picture, with home-grown companies making significant contributions across key strategic export sectors.
"Our half-year analysis paints a more complete picture. It shows that Malaysian-owned companies are also making significant contributions across most of our strategic export sectors," he said.
Reezal said Malaysia's rising competitiveness is reflected in its climb to 15th place in the IMD World Competitiveness Ranking from 23rd in 2025, its strongest performance in a decade, signalling deeper structural improvements rather than a temporary recovery.
"Equally significant, Malaysia recorded trade surpluses with 158 trading partners, with 92 posting wider surpluses than a year ago. We also achieved net trade surpluses across 14 major product categories, underscoring the resilience and diversity of our export base across markets and industries," he said.
The findings come as Malaysia posted its strongest-ever trade performance for the first half of 2026 despite heightened geopolitical tensions and an uncertain global trade environment.
Total trade rose 22.4 per cent year-on-year to a record RM1.796 trillion, while exports climbed 27.5 per cent to RM971.59 billion, the fastest growth since 2021. The trade surplus surged 159.8 per cent to RM147.15 billion, equivalent to 94 per cent of the surplus recorded for the whole of 2025.
Matrade's first-half trade analysis, released alongside the Statistics Department's Monthly External Trade Statistics on July 20, examined the structural drivers underpinning the country's export resilience and highlighted the growing contribution of Malaysian-owned companies to its trade performance.
Samuel Tan, founder and chief executive officer of Olive Tree Property Consultants, said the latest trade data signals a meaningful shift in Malaysia's export landscape, with home-grown companies strengthening their presence in higher value-added industries alongside multinational corporations.
He said Malaysian firms have spent years building their capabilities through greater investment in technology, stronger supply chain integration and expanding their reach into overseas markets.
"The latest trade figures show Malaysia's export base is becoming broader and more balanced. Local companies are no longer just supporting multinational manufacturers but are increasingly exporting their own products and services to global markets," he told Business Times.
Tan said Malaysia's record trade performance in the first half of 2026 also suggests external demand has remained resilient despite geopolitical tensions and the conflict in the Middle East.
He described exports to the United States as particularly encouraging, noting that while shipments eased slightly from the previous month, they were still 108.6 per cent higher than a year earlier.
"That indicates fears over US President Donald Trump's tariffs have not materially weakened Malaysia's exports to the US. Bilateral trade continues to perform strongly despite concerns over protectionist measures," he said.
Tan added that the growing contribution of Malaysian-owned exporters reflects a broader and more diversified industrial base, reducing the country's dependence on multinational companies as the main source of export growth.
He said many local firms have moved further up the value chain by raising productivity, adopting automation and expanding into new international markets, making Malaysia's export sector more resilient over the longer term.
AI Boom Powers Malaysia's Export Surge
Reezal said the country's export performance was supported by two major global tailwinds – the surge in artificial intelligence (AI)-driven demand for electrical and electronics (E&E) products and sustained global energy demand.
The E&E sector remained Malaysia's largest export contributor, with exports surging 42.5 per cent year-on-year to RM467.95 billion, accounting for 48.2 per cent of total exports. Semiconductors made up 73.7 per cent of E&E exports, supported by robust demand from the United States, Singapore, the European Union and Japan.
"Our energy exports continue to demonstrate Malaysia's strategic importance in global energy supply chains. Led by Petroliam Nasional Bhd (Petronas), which holds full ownership of the sector's trade value, petroleum products expanded by 27.4 per cent, while liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports increased by 12.4 per cent.
"This performance was supported not only by elevated global energy prices but also by a 21.4 per cent increase in LNG export volumes, signalling sustained international demand," he said in a statement.
Reezal said Malaysia also continues to strengthen its competitive position across the palm oil value chain, with Malaysian-owned companies accounting for about 70 per cent ownership across agriculture and edible oil refining, as well as more than 63 per cent ownership in downstream palm-based oleochemicals, industrial fatty acids and biodiesel.
That competitive edge translated into stronger export performance, with palm oil-based manufactured products rising 7.1 per cent to RM20.83 billion in the first half of 2026, driven mainly by higher oleochemical exports.
He added that Malaysian-owned companies account for more than 72 per cent of the chemicals and chemical products industry, spanning speciality chemicals, polymers, fertilisers, cleaning preparations, polyethylene resins and personal care products, highlighting the increasing sophistication and depth of Malaysia's domestic industrial capabilities.
"Taken together, across nine of Malaysia's top ten export sectors, these findings revealed that Malaysian-owned companies hold more than 40 per cent ownership, demonstrating that our export success is increasingly driven by competitive, globally connected local enterprises," he said.
The analysis also showed that Malaysia's export diversification strategy continues to deliver strong results across both traditional and emerging markets.
Exports to traditional markets remained robust, with shipments to the United States surging 54.8 per cent year-on-year to RM173.37 billion.
Exports to Asean rose 18.6 per cent to RM259.60 billion, while shipments to the European Union increased 28.4 per cent to RM75.85 billion, China climbed 23.3 per cent to RM107.28 billion, Taiwan jumped 66.5 per cent to RM65.44 billion and Hong Kong SAR gained 48.6 per cent to RM67.68 billion.
At the same time, exports to non-traditional markets across Africa, Central Asia, Latin America and Oceania expanded a combined 13.3 per cent to RM72.15 billion.
Among the strongest performers were Sudan, where exports surged 222.3 per cent to RM219.7 million, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (+116.4 per cent; RM137.7 million), Angola (+125.4 per cent; RM531 million), Venezuela (+77.3 per cent; RM30.3 million), Brazil (+30 per cent; RM2.31 billion), Turkmenistan (+39.7 per cent; RM48.7 million) and New Zealand (+29 per cent; RM3.47 billion).
Exports to free trade agreement (FTA) partners climbed 21.5 per cent to RM616.55 billion, representing 63.5 per cent of Malaysia's total exports.
Nineteen of the country's 24 FTA partners recorded growth, led by the Republic of Korea (+31.5 per cent; RM32.19 billion), Japan (+9.1 per cent; RM41.97 billion), Australia (+9 per cent; RM5.66 billion), Mexico (+49.6 per cent; RM20.03 billion) and the United Kingdom (+36 per cent; RM5.66 billion).
Exports to Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) markets rose 19 per cent to RM470.41 billion, while shipments to Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) economies increased 17 per cent to RM272.61 billion.
Reezal said this underscores the importance of Malaysia's participation in major regional trade agreements in strengthening long-term trade resilience, adding that the country's export momentum has translated into stronger domestic economic performance.
Exports contributed to Malaysia's 5.6 per cent gross domestic product (GDP) growth in the first half of the year, while the Industrial Production Index rose 8.4 per cent in May, supported by export-oriented industries and electronics manufacturing.
"As encouraging as this half-year has been, Matrade does not view it as a moment of complacency. The situation in the Middle East remains fluid, and global supply chains will continue to require careful navigation in the months ahead," he said.
Economist Dr Geoffrey Williams said Malaysia's latest trade figures indicate that global demand has remained more resilient than expected despite geopolitical tensions and the conflict in the Middle East.
He said export performance to the US was particularly encouraging, with shipments continuing to show strong growth.
Although exports to the US eased slightly on a month-on-month basis, they still surged 108.6 per cent from a year earlier, he said.

Title: Ride-hailing, delivery demand holds despite cost squeeze
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysians are tightening their spending when using ride-hailing and food delivery services as rising living costs squeeze household budgets, prompting consumers to be more selective without significantly weakening demand, industry players said.
A Rakuten Insight survey found 82 per cent of 1,003 respondents would adjust their usage if prices rise further due to higher fuel costs.
eHailing Malaysia Coalition (GEM) chief activist Masrizal Mahidin said the shift reflects greater focus on value, promotions and cost savings rather than a decline in demand, as these services remain part of Malaysians' daily routines.
"Consumers are now more cautious when making decisions. They are reducing unnecessary trips, waiting for promotional periods, choosing non-peak hours, comparing prices across platforms and are increasingly inclined to seek cheaper alternatives," he told Business Times.
Masrizal said the survey should serve as a reminder that Malaysian consumers remain highly sensitive to price changes, particularly amid ongoing cost-of-living pressures.
It showed that 28 per cent of respondents would switch to cheaper alternatives such as public transport, drive their own car, or cook at home if prices increase further. Another 27 per cent said they would reduce their usage, while 17 per cent would only use the services when promotions are available.
Only 8 per cent said they would continue using the services as usual, with convenience being the main reason, while 10 per cent would stop using them altogether.
Masrizal said long-term growth requires a balance between consumers, platforms and drivers.
"The solution cannot rely solely on fare increases. What is needed is structural reform within the industry to ensure a balance between consumer affordability, platform competitiveness and the welfare of gig workers," he said.
Economist Doris Liew said changes in ride-hailing and food delivery demand could serve as an early indicator of softer private consumption, as these services are among the discretionary purchases households can adjust quickly when incomes come under pressure.
However, she noted that broader economic indicators have yet to point towards a significant slowdown in Malaysian consumer spending.
"In the first quarter of 2026, real private consumption grew by 4.7 per cent year on year, with transport spending rising 9.2 per cent and restaurants and hotels by 12.9 per cent," she said.
Liew said trends in e-hailing and food delivery should be assessed alongside wider indicators such as public transport usage, retail activity, employment, wages and consumer sentiment.
"Things like weaker delivery orders alongside stronger restaurant activity may simply indicate consumers shifting back to dining out rather than cutting spending altogether," she said.
inDrive Asia-Pacific director Mark Tolley said the company has observed greater price sensitivity among users, although demand for ride-hailing remains supported by its role in daily mobility.
"Passengers are becoming more selective about the journeys they take and the value they receive, while drivers must account for fuel, maintenance, insurance and other operating expenses when assessing whether a trip is economically viable," he said.
Tolley expects underlying demand for ride-hailing to remain resilient over the next 12 months, supported by daily commuting needs, tourism, airport transfers and first- and last-mile connectivity.
However, consumers may become more selective, particularly when it comes to discretionary journeys or deliveries, if prices rise significantly, he said.
The key challenge ahead is balancing consumer affordability with the need to ensure platforms and gig workers remain financially sustainable.

Title: Growth wave demands bigger power supply
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia will need to add substantial power generation capacity over the coming years as electricity demand accelerates, fuelled by investments in data centres, semiconductor manufacturing and other energy-intensive industries, according to Mitsubishi Power Asia-Pacific.
Its managing director and chief executive Akihiro Ondo said the rapid expansion of digital infrastructure, particularly data centres in Johor, is emerging as a major driver of electricity demand, alongside continued economic growth.
"In Malaysia, electricity demand is growing significantly due to stable economic growth and newly installed data centres, especially in Johor," he told Business Times.
"As demand continues to grow, Malaysia needs a significant addition to its power supply capacity," he said.
Ondo said Mitsubishi Power, which has been involved in Malaysia's power sector for more than 60 years, is working closely with utilities to prepare for future demand.
The company has signed reservation agreements with Tenaga Nasional Bhd (TNB) for six gas turbines and with Malakoff Corp Bhd for four turbines, while also participating in a power station project in Miri, Sarawak.
He said the reservation agreements are intended to secure future equipment deliveries amid rising demand for power generation equipment globally.
"These agreements are intended to secure the delivery of gas turbines to TNB. To move forward with the installation or construction of a power plant, subsequent agreements will be required. These agreements will build on the reservation agreements and form the basis for project execution," he said.
Ondo said Malaysia is not alone in facing rising electricity demand, noting that countries worldwide are expanding generation capacity as investments in artificial intelligence (AI), hyperscale data centres, advanced manufacturing and electrification gather pace.
"If we look at the global market, electricity demand has massively increased in the United States due to hyperscalers' investments for new data centres," he said.
Ondo said investment in gas turbine-related projects is also booming.
To secure sufficient resources or equipment, long-term planning, and proactive and strategic dialogue with stakeholders such as TNB or Malakoff are essential, he said.
"That is the most important factor. We need to act early to mitigate the gap between rising demand and existing capacity," he said.
Ondo believes Malaysia has a solid foundation, with well-developed power generation, transmission and distribution networks, but said additional capacity will be needed to support the country's long-term economic ambitions.
Beyond data centres, he expects rising electric vehicle adoption, semiconductor investments and broader industrial expansion to drive electricity consumption higher over the next decade.
Despite the country's growing focus on renewable energy, Ondo said natural gas will remain a critical component of Malaysia's power mix because it provides the flexibility needed to complement intermittent renewable sources such as solar and wind.
"Unlike solar and wind power, gas turbines can be deployed quickly when electricity demand rises or when renewable output falls due to weather conditions.
"In case renewables cannot generate power because of rain, a lack of sunlight, or changes in wind direction, open-cycle gas turbines can be started much faster than other applications," he said.
He added that natural gas remains an important transition fuel, particularly for countries such as Malaysia that already possess natural gas resources and supporting infrastructure.
Beyond natural gas, Mitsubishi Power is also developing technologies that can utilise hydrogen in power generation.
Ondo said the six turbines reserved for TNB, four units for Malakoff and the Sarawak project, are already capable of co-firing hydrogen.
While hydrogen and other low-carbon technologies remain part of the long-term energy transition, Ondo said the immediate priority across Southeast Asia is ensuring adequate and reliable electricity supply.
He said governments and utilities are currently focused on energy security, affordability and resilience as electricity consumption continues to rise.

Title: Bar's appeal over Najib's reduced sentence among key court hearings this week
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR:  Several  court proceedings involving prominent political figures and major corruption cases are set to unfold in the coming week.
On Friday, the Court of Appeal is expected to fix a date to deliver its judgment in the Malaysian Bar's appeal challenging the Pardons Board's decision to halve former prime minister Datuk Seri Najib Razak's prison sentence and reduce his fine in the SRC International case.
A three-member panel chaired by Judge Lim Chong Fong had on July 31 reserved its decision in the appeal, which challenges the High Court's earlier refusal to grant leave for judicial review of the board's decision.
The Malaysian Bar has sought a declaration that the Pardons Board's decision on Jan 29, 2024, to halve Najib's prison sentence — resulting in his early release slated for Aug 23, 2028 — is illegal, unconstitutional and void.
It is also seeking a declaration that the reduction of Najib's fine from RM210 million to RM50 million is similarly illegal, unconstitutional and void.
During submissions at the Court of Appeal on July 31, the Bar's lawyer Yeo Yang Poh argued that accountability was a fundamental pillar of the justice system and that the Pardons Board's functions should be subject to judicial scrutiny, adding that the board must be held accountable to the people.
The following week will see two further significant hearings.
The Klang Sessions Court is scheduled on Aug 11 to hear a criminal mention in the sedition case involving blogger Wan Muhammad Azri Wan Deris, better known as Papagomo.
The mention follows a recent High Court decision that overturned his acquittal and ordered him to enter his defence against charges of posting allegedly seditious statements against the government on Facebook.
Two days later on Aug 13, the High Court will hear a major application by the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission seeking a prohibition and restraining order against Toh Puan Na'imah Abdul Khalid, the widow of former finance minister Tun Daim Zainuddin, over the alleged management of substantial offshore assets.
Meanwhile, the ongoing corruption trial of former prime minister Tan Sri Muhyiddin Yassin in the Jana Wibawa case at the Special Corruption High Court is on recess during the week of Aug 10-14, with  hearings scheduled to resume from Aug 17 to 21.

Title: DAP warned against Cabinet exit after electoral setbacks [WATCH]
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Quitting the cabinet may help DAP rebuild credibility among its traditional supporters after successive electoral defeats, but the political cost would outweigh any benefits, said  Dr Ong Kian Ming.
"It could cost the party control of the Penang  government and its participation in the Selangor  government," he said.
Ong said such a move, which has been discussed since DAP failed to win a single seat in the Sabah election, would also make it difficult for the party to campaign for Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim in the next general election.
The former Bangi member of parliament from DAP said this when asked about the party's   options after Pakatan Harapan's loss in Saturday's Negri Sembilan election.
One of the biggest headlines  was secretary-general Anthony Loke's defeat in Chennah, a seat he had held since 2013.
DAP also lost the Repah seat.
Ong said the outcome stemmed from several factors, including DAP's inability to mobilise its supporters, particularly Chinese voters, at the same rate as Malay voters.
He also said PH struggled to counter the Malay unity narrative put forward by Barisan Nasional and Perikatan Nasional.
In the aftermath of Saturday's polls, Loke said he was considering resigning as Negri Sembilan DAP chief, though Ong said neither that nor exiting the Anwar-led administration would produce immediate results.
"The DAP congress on Aug 16 will present an opportunity for delegates to debate the party's direction, but leaving the cabinet should not be viewed as an immediate solution," he said.
DAP deputy secretary-general Ramkarpal Singh said it would be unfair  to pin the blame on Loke for the loss in Negri Sembilan.
"There are a number of factors," Ramkarpal told the
New Straits Times
.
"In terms of DAP's performance, Loke led the party well in Negri Sembilan."
Ramkarpal said  while losing the two seats was disappointing, other factors had also played a part in the results.
"Our performance as a  coalition has to be taken into account. We also have to see if we've met the demands of voters, not just in Negri Sembilan but also at the federal level."
He said these were matters that needed to be looked into ahead of the party's  congress.
Ramkarpal added that DAP respected the outcome of the polls and thanked voters for their support.
Some observers  said the way forward for DAP could lie outside PH, but Universiti Sains Malaysia political analyst Professor Datuk Dr Sivamurugan Pandian warned that this was a double-edged sword.
"Leaving could create a clearer opposition identity, but it could also cost DAP influence and make it appear responsible for political instability.
"The bigger issue is whether DAP can reform within the coalition," he told the NST.
He said while some form of restructuring was necessary, withdrawing from the coalition or Anwar's cabinet might not  be the answer.
Sivamurugan said DAP should use the Aug 16 congress to reassess its strategy, leadership and electoral base before making such a major decision.

Title: Israeli strikes kill 13 in Gaza
Article:
GAZA CITY: Israeli strikes on Gaza hit multiple residential buildings and killed at least 13 people, authorities said on Sunday, despite Hamas saying it had agreed to the latest stage of a deal to end the war.
Hamas said on Friday it had agreed to a plan championed by US President Donald Trump that includes provisions for handing over its weapons and the gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces from the Gaza Strip.
Israel has yet to officially comment on the agreement, but a political source told AFP "that there will be no withdrawal whatsoever" without Hamas's "genuine disarmament".
Gaza's civil defence rescue service, which operates under Hamas authority, said on Sunday that eight people were killed in strikes around midnight that hit multiple residential buildings, while five others were killed later in the day.
In one overnight attack near the central Gaza Strip, a man and his wife were killed and several others were wounded when an Israeli military helicopter struck an apartment, a civil defence spokesman said.
An elderly man and a child were killed in another attack on an apartment west of Gaza City, while three people, including a child, were killed in a strike on a residential building northwest of Khan Younis in the southern Gaza Strip.
"One person was killed and four others injured in an Israeli drone strike targeting a group of civilians near a camp for displaced people in Jabalia refugee camp, northern Gaza Strip," he said.
A couple and their child were killed in a strike on an apartment west of Gaza City at dawn, the spokesman said, adding that the woman was pregnant.
Two others were killed in an Israeli drone strike on their vehicle in Deir al-Balah in the central Gaza Strip, he said, with Al-Aqsa Martyrs' Hospital saying they were brothers.
Hamas politburo member Ghazi Hamad condemned the strikes on Sunday and told AFP that "Israel's escalation in Gaza today confirms that Israel doesn't want to reach an agreement".
On Saturday, authorities reported that eight people had been killed in strikes that damaged a hospital's medical supplies and targeted a rooftop. The Israeli army said two of the strikes targeted members of the Army of Islam and Islamic Jihad fighter groups.
Nickolay Mladenov, High Representative of the Board of Peace, the international body overseeing the US-backed Gaza plan, said the latest strikes had compromised diplomatic efforts towards the implementation of the plan.
"Two days of strikes across Gaza have killed civilians and destroyed medical supplies that people depend on," he wrote on X.
"This comes after intense efforts by the Board of Peace and the mediators... to bring the Palestinian factions in Gaza to agree to a Roadmap on the full implementation of President Trump's plan. Both parties carry obligations under the Comprehensive Plan."

Title: Negri polls expose PH's struggle to win Malay support [WATCH]
Article:
SEREMBAN: The outcome of the Negri Sembilan election   exposed deeper challenges for Pakatan Harapan, particularly its ability to retain and expand Malay support.
Results show  Barisan Nasional  emerging as the biggest winner with 18 seats, followed by PH with 11 and Perikatan Nasional with seven.
Umno secured 16 seats for BN, while MCA won two.
Within PH, DAP scored nine victories, followed by PKR with two seats.
PN's seven seats were secured by Pas (four) and Parti Wawasan Negara (three).
Bersatu  failed to win any seats.
Universiti Teknologi Malaysia Faculty of Social Sciences and Humanities associate professor Dr Mazlan Ali said the outcome should serve as a warning  for PH, as voters appeared to be influenced by broader political narratives beyond state government performance.
He said the defeat of former menteri besar Datuk Seri Aminuddin Harun in Linggi showed that even a government with a strong   record was not immune to wider political shifts.
"The Malay-Islam narrative appeared to play a significant role in shaping their choices," he told the
New Straits Times.
"BN and PN combined their Malay support.
"Apart from Pas' traditional supporters, Pas also gained support from BN voters."
Universiti Malaya's Department of Political Science, Public Administration and Development Studies senior lecturer Dr Mohammad Tawfik Yaakub said the result could be viewed as a   referendum   on the state government and the PH's federal leadership.
He said the defeats of Aminuddin and DAP secretary-general Anthony Loke indicated that national issues, perceptions towards the federal government and confidence in PH's leadership had influenced voters.
"However, this was not a total rejection of PH, as candidate appeal, constituency dynamics and local strategies remained important factors."
Tawfik said the BN-PN pact created a more organised challenge against PH.
"The strength of Umno's machinery, Pas' influence, local candidates and rural voter mobilisation also played a significant role."
For PH, the result exposed a gap between DAP's ability to retain support and   PKR and Amanah's struggle to attract Malay voters.
DAP retained nine seats — Bahau, Nilai, Lobak, Temiang, Bukit Kepayang, Rahang, Mambau, Seremban Jaya and Lukut.
However, several of these constituencies continue to reflect DAP's reliance on mixed and non-Malay support bases.
Mambau has a Chinese voter share of 45.4 per cent,   Bahau has 45.6 per cent and Bukit Kepayang has 41.9 per cent.
Seremban Jaya and Rahang also have significant Chinese voter presence at 37.8 per cent and 38.1 per cent, respectively.
Tawfik said PH remained  dependent on urban and non-Malay support but lacked   Malay support.
He said DAP's defeat in Chennah, a mixed constituency, was  significant as it suggested the party's cross-community appeal was under pressure.
Loke lost Chennah to MCA candidate Siow Kong Choon by   688 votes, while PH also narrowly lost Repah to BN by 444 votes.
The setbacks came after DAP suffered electoral losses in Sabah and Johor.
Tawfik said the defeat placed pressure on Loke, who is not only DAP secretary-general but also the party's Negri Sembilan chairman.
He said while the loss did not mean Loke must relinquish his national position, stepping aside as state chairman would be   a gesture of accountability.
The DAP National Congress on Aug 16 is expected to become an important  post-election review platform to discuss grassroots rebuilding and   electoral strategy.
International Islamic University Malaysia political scientist Associate Professor Dr Syaza Shukri said the BN-PN cooperation was an effective strategy to consolidate Malay support previously divided between the two blocs.
"In the 2023 state election, many Malay-majority seats were closely contested between BN and PN, showing that Malay support was strong but fragmented. This time,  cooperation helped consolidate those votes and created a stronger narrative."
However, she said the result did not  mean PH had completely lost its Malay supporters.
"PH previously contested with support from other Malay-based parties, whether BN in 2023 or Bersatu in 2018.
"The core Malay supporters of PH may remain, but the coalition has lost some of the additional Malay votes it gained through those partnerships."

Title: The Blue Wave's biggest test begins now
Article:
THE outcome of the Negri Sembilan election on Aug 1 confirms that the "Blue Wave" has evolved from campaign rhetoric into a measurable electoral reality.
Together, Barisan Nasional and  and Perikatan Nasional now command 25 seats, giving the alliance a two-thirds majority and bringing the era of  Pakatan Harapan-led administrations to an end after two terms.
Voter turnout reached 72.64 per cent involving 646,084 registered voters, an increase from 68.35 per cent recorded in 2023.
The defeats of prominent PH leaders in Chennah and Linggi were symbols of a broader political shift.
Nevertheless, these outcomes do not establish that all non-Malay voters shifted towards BN.
Even so, the demographic pattern is evident. BN strengthened its position across Malay-majority, rural and semi-urban constituencies, while PH largely retained support in selected urban seats.
MCA's victories in Chennah and Repah illustrate that BN can  penetrate mixed constituencies when effective local machinery, credible candidates and coordinated vote transfers operate simultaneously.
At the same time, MIC's inability to secure representation demonstrates that BN's  recovery remains uneven.
A decisive factor behind the outcome was the coordination between BN and PN, which reduced the fragmentation of Malay votes and enabled both coalitions to concentrate resources on different target constituencies.
However, the victory should not be interpreted as evidence that the partnership is free from internal challenges.
Bersatu contested independently and failed to secure seats, whereas its splinter party, Wawasan, won three of the four seats it contested.
These results expose  questions regarding Bersatu's leadership, organisational identity and long-term political relevance.
For PH, the defeat cannot be explained solely through identity politics. Although ethnic narratives may have influenced certain segments of the electorate, broader issues  also contributed.
PH must undertake a comprehensive review of its campaign machinery, candidate selection, economic messaging  and engagement with middle-ground voters.
The BN-PN victory also brings constitutional responsibilities.
The formation of the state government and the appointment of the menteri besar remain subject to the constitutional framework of Negri Sembilan and the discretion of the Yang di-Pertuan Besar.
A two-thirds majority provides substantial legislative authority, yet without transparency, institutional accountability and respect for constitutional processes, electoral success can quickly become a governance burden.
The national implications are considerable, although not uniform. Melaka and Pahang appear most likely to experience spillover effects because of BN's organisational strength.
Perak and Negri  Sembilan  demonstrate that mixed constituencies can change when Malay support consolidates while PH's non-Malay margins weaken.
Selangor and Penang require different strategic approaches because of their stronger urban composition.
Kedah, Kelantan, and Terengganu remain heavily influenced by Pas, while Sabah and Sarawak cannot be evaluated using Peninsular assumptions.
Post-election strategy should begin with three priorities.
First, BN and PN should publish a transparent governing framework covering portfolios, shared policies and dispute-resolution mechanisms.
Second, PH should undertake a rigorous data-driven post-mortem rather than relying on revised political slogans.
Third, the Election Commission and independent researchers should expand polling-stream publication so claims regarding demographic voting shifts can be tested empirically.
Without stronger evidence, political narratives will continue to outpace   facts.
For investors, changes in government are not the principal concern; policy uncertainty is.
Any incoming administration must preserve project continuity, fiscal discipline, procurement transparency and regulatory certainty.
Political victory acquires lasting economic value only when translated into sustainable development, employment creation  and enduring public confidence.
Ultimately, the Negri Sembilan election confirms the existence of a "Blue Wave" within the state but does not, by itself, establish an automatic nationwide domino effect.
BN possesses renewed momentum, PN  benefited strategically, PH has lost ground and Bersatu has suffered a decisive setback.
To transform electoral success into lasting political realignment, BN and PN must govern with greater discipline than they campaigned — remaining united without becoming overbearing, decisive without becoming divisive and effective without weakening the institutions that underpin Malaysia's constitutional democracy.
The writer is a political and economic analyst

Title: Iran says close to Hormuz deal with Oman after US suspends attack plan
Article:
TEHERAN: Iran on Sunday said it was nearing a deal with Oman over a new route through the Strait of Hormuz, hours after the US called off major strikes to allow for diplomacy.
US President Donald Trump said on Saturday that his country and Israel had agreed to hold off on new strikes on Iran, saying the "perimeters" of a deal were there.
The foes have been at war since February 28, when the US and Israel launched surprise strikes against Iran, although months of on-and-off diplomacy have led to periods of relative calm.
Following a return to strikes last month, fears had mounted that the fighting could escalate once again. Trump had threatened to hit Iran "very hard" and was reportedly considering renewed attacks, including against energy infrastructure, with US embassies across the region on alert.
But the US leader appeared to have changed course after a flurry of diplomacy, including speaking with Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
Trump said "we have just been asked by Iran, and other Middle Eastern Countries, to hold off any attack in that the perimeters of a deal has been agreed to".
"Based on this request, I have agreed, for the future benefit of the WORLD and, likewise, the survival of a successful and prosperous Iran, to cancel the attack, subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL," Trump posted on his Truth Social platform.
It was not immediately clear what the US president meant about the state of negotiations. Iranian media denied that Teheran had asked Trump not to strike.
EXCHANGE OF VIEWS
Iranian lawmaker Hassan Ghashghavi, spokesman for the parliament's national security commission, said on Sunday that mediators were trying to revive the so-called Islamabad memorandum of understanding, which was agreed in June.
That memorandum was not intended as a final peace deal, but as a stepping stone to negotiations on a comprehensive agreement, although it did include provisions on Hormuz.
"They know that the main issue and, in fact, the key to the matter right now is the issue of the Strait of Hormuz, so yes, there is an exchange of views," Ghashghavi said.
Posting on X, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said: "We must strive to compel the enemy to remain committed to what it has signed."
Hormuz, a vital route for global oil and gas supplies, has been at the centre of the failed diplomatic efforts so far.
Before the war, there was free passage for all vessels, but Iran closed the strait during the war and now insists on retaining control and charging tolls, something the US rejects.
Trump said any deal would have to include the "Immediate, Complete and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT, and an end to Iran's nuclear threat."
The US president said at the start of the conflict that the war was necessary to deal with Iran's nuclear programme. Western nations accuse Iran of seeking a bomb, although Teheran insists the programme is entirely civilian in nature.
The dispute over the Strait of Hormuz sparked the return to strikes last month, as Teheran refused to let ships travel any route other than one that hugs the Iranian coast.
On Sunday, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei told state television that a deal was close with Oman, which sits on the other side of the strait, over a new route through it.
"We are now going to reach an understanding on a route acceptable to both sides – neither the northern route nor the southern route – but one that respects the sovereign rights of both sides and safeguards our national interests and security," he said.
He insisted, however, that such an agreement did not mean the reopening of the strait.
Maritime trade tracking firm Kpler said on Friday that traffic through Hormuz had dropped sharply.

Title: Trump says new Iran talks to begin Monday after calling off strikes
Article:
WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump said negotiations with Iran will begin on Monday after he decided to hold off on new "disastrous" strikes against the Islamic republic to pursue a deal.
"Obviously, they don't want to be attacked. They knew the extent of the attack because they saw it forming," Trump told reporters on Sunday aboard Air Force One.
"Now what we're doing is we're talking to them in the form of a negotiation. It begins tomorrow afternoon," he said, without providing further details on the venue of the talks or the participants.
On Saturday, the US president pulled back from threats of a massive attack against Iran, which he said would have been the biggest since World War II, saying the "perimeter" of a deal was there.
In his comments on Sunday, explaining his decision-making, Trump said he had been asked by Iran as well as US partners Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar to hold off on the strikes.
"When the allies asked to call it off, you've got to sort of say, 'Well, let's see.' And the reason they ask is they think there's a deal," Trump said.
[[nid:1503037]]
"There's a deal on (the Strait of) Hormuz, and then there will be a deal on the nuclear, or you might call it the denuclearisation of Iran."
He reiterated that the scale of the planned strikes would have been "the biggest attack since World War II".
"It would take many, many years to ever build it back if it could — I don't think it would even be buildable," Trump asserted.
He said Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman had also urged against the strikes, warning of possible unintended consequences.
"I mean, will they be flooded with people pouring into their country and disaster? A lot of bad things can happen," Trump said.
The war began on Feb 28 when the US and Israel launched surprise strikes against Iran, although months of on-and-off diplomacy have led to periods of relative calm.
A previous ceasefire deal, including the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz — a vital conduit for global energy supplies — fell through, and Iran has since tightened its control over the vital waterway as the two countries resumed attacks against each other in recent weeks.

Title: 2,000 take part in Sarawak Jom Heboh run
Article:

As a light drizzle fell, Media Prima Omnia chief operating officer Datuk Mohd Efendi Omar flagged off the participants, comprising people all ages, including families, youths and health-conscious individuals.

Title: Trump says US support for Japanese yen a 'signal of friendship'
Article:
WASHINGTON: President Donald Trump on Sunday confirmed that the United States had intervened to support the Japanese yen, calling the move a "signal of friendship" that would financially benefit the US and the world economy.
The Financial Times reported on Friday that the US Treasury had jointly intervened with Japan to prop up the yen for the first time in nearly three decades.
Asked aboard Air Force One why the US was moving to support Japan's currency, Trump said: "Because we have a good relationship with Japan."
The US will see "financial benefit" from the move and "it's also good for the world economy", Trump insisted, but "it was really more than anything else, it was a signal of friendship".
"We're very strong — very, very strong financially. They are, you know, they have a weakening yen, and they wanted a little bit of help. And we're always there for Japan. Japan's been very good to us, with the exception, of course, of Pearl Harbor," the president said.
[[nid:1502984]]
The Financial Times reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that the Federal Reserve Bank of New York had taken the unusual step of selling euros to buy yen on behalf of the US Treasury on Friday.
The intervention came after the yen slid to 163.24 per dollar last month, its weakest level since 1986, as higher US interest rates, rising oil prices and persistent capital outflows weighed on the currency.
Washington's move came as the yen rebounded sharply last week, fuelling speculation that Japanese authorities had also intervened in currency markets.
Analysts cited by the Financial Times estimated Japan's intervention may have totalled about 8.45 trillion yen (US$52.8 billion).
The Nikkei business daily put the amount at between 6 trillion and 7 trillion yen.
According to the Financial Times, the move would be the first coordinated US-Japan effort to support the yen since 1998.
